mushrooms.name: Mushrooms (button, shiitake)

sections.whatItOffers: White (button) mushrooms are very low in energy and give potassium, along with a little protein.
sections.practicalServing: 1 cup pieces or slices (USDA: 1 cup = 70 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Slice raw into salads, or sauté, roast or add to soups, omelettes and stir-fries. Cooking them in a dry pan first lets the water cook off so they brown.
sections.cycleRelevance: No cycle-phase claim is made for mushrooms. They are a low-energy way to add bulk and potassium to a meal at any point in the cycle.

source.portion: 1 cup pieces or slices (USDA: 1 cup = 70 g)

brussels-sprouts.name: Brussels sprouts

sections.whatItOffers: Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-family buds that are rich in vitamin C and vitamin K, with some folate and fibre.
sections.practicalServing: ½ cup cooked (USDA: 0.5 cup = 78 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Roast halved sprouts with olive oil until browned, shred them raw into slaws, or steam until just tender. Overcooking makes them bitter and sulphurous.
sections.cycleRelevance: Vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron from the same meal (NIH ODS), so sprouts pair well with beans or lentils. No phase-specific claim is made.

source.usdaDescription: Brussels sprouts, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt
source.portion: ½ cup cooked (USDA: 0.5 cup = 78 g)

keyNutrients.referenceNote: Adequate intake for women 19 and over is 90 µg; shown as an amount only. See the note on blood thinners.

cautions.text: Brussels sprouts contains vitamin K. If you take warfarin or a similar blood thinner, keep your intake steady and tell your clinician.
cautions.source: NIH ODS Vitamin K (interaction with warfarin and other anticoagulants)

chard.name: Chard

sections.whatItOffers: Swiss chard is a leafy green with plenty of vitamin A and vitamin K, magnesium, some vitamin C and a little plant iron.
sections.practicalServing: ½ cup chopped, cooked (USDA: 1 cup = 175 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Sauté the leaves and stems separately, since the stems take longer. Stir the leaves into soups and eggs, or bake them into gratins with a squeeze of lemon.
sections.cycleRelevance: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Chard adds some plant iron, which is absorbed less readily than iron from meat; vitamin C in the same meal helps.

eggplant.name: Eggplant

sections.whatItOffers: Eggplant is a mild, soft-textured vegetable that is very low in energy, with a little fibre and potassium. It is mostly valued for its texture rather than for concentrated nutrients.
sections.practicalServing: ½ cup cooked cubes (USDA: 1 cup of 1 in cubes = 99 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Roast or grill slices, blend into dips such as baba ganoush, or stew in curries and ratatouille. It soaks up oil when fried, so roasting or grilling uses less.
sections.cycleRelevance: No cycle-phase claim is made for eggplant. It is a low-energy vegetable that adds bulk and fibre to a meal at any time.

collard.name: Collard

sections.practicalServing: ½ cup chopped, cooked (USDA: 1 cup = 190 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Simmer or braise until tender, shred into soups and stews, or use blanched leaves as wraps.

green-bell-pepper.name: Green bell pepper

sections.whatItOffers: A green bell pepper is crisp and mild, and one medium pepper has about 96 mg of vitamin C, more than the 75 mg daily reference for adult women, plus a little potassium.
sections.practicalServing: 1 medium pepper (USDA: 1 medium = 119 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Eat it raw in strips or salads, roast or stuff it, or sauté it in stir-fries and stews. Served with beans or lentils, its vitamin C helps your body absorb plant iron.
sections.cycleRelevance: Vitamin C improves the absorption of plant iron (NIH ODS), a useful pairing for anyone who menstruates and relies on plant foods for iron. No phase-specific claim is made.

white-potato.name: White potato

sections.whatItOffers: A baked potato eaten with its skin is a filling starchy vegetable and a notable source of potassium (about 926 mg in a medium potato), with vitamin C, magnesium and fibre.
sections.practicalServing: 1 medium baked potato with skin (USDA: 1 medium = 173 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Bake whole and eat with the skin, roast wedges, or boil and cool for potato salad. The USDA record is for flesh and skin together.
sections.cycleRelevance: Potassium has an adequate intake of 2,600 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS), and a medium baked potato supplies about 36% of it. No cycle-phase claim is made.

lettuce.name: Lettuce (Bibb, Boston, romaine)

sections.whatItOffers: Romaine is a crisp lettuce with a lot of vitamin A and folate for very few calories: two cups of shredded leaves give about 59% of the vitamin A and 32% of the folate reference, plus vitamin K.
sections.practicalServing: 2 cups shredded (USDA: 1 cup shredded = 47 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Use it as the base of salads, grill halves, or use the leaves as crunchy wraps. Dress it just before serving so it stays crisp.
